```{r}
library(vroom)
library(tidyverse)
library(forecast)
library(patchwork)
library(lmtest)
library(prophet)

predictors <- c("Income", "Production", "Savings", "Unemployment")

dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)

data <- vroom("C:/Users/aidan/Downloads/CompanyGrowth.csv") %>%
  mutate(Qrtr = factor(Qrtr))

data_all <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(PctGrowth), if_all(all_of(predictors), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
  mutate(q  = as.numeric(as.character(Qrtr)),
         ds = as.Date(paste(Year, (q - 1) * 3 + 1, 1, sep = "-")),
         y  = PctGrowth) %>%
  arrange(ds)

tail(data_all)
```

```{r}
make_future <- function(train, end_date = as.Date("2025-10-01")) {
  tibble(ds = seq(max(train$ds), end_date, by = "quarter")[-1]) %>%
    mutate(Year = year(ds),
           Qrtr = factor(quarter(ds), levels = levels(train$Qrtr)))
}

future_all <- make_future(data_all)
future_all   # CHECK: these are the quarters being projected

ts_of <- function(x, df) ts(x, start = c(df$Year[1], df$q[1]), frequency = 4)
mae   <- function(actual, pred) mean(abs(actual - pred))
```

```{r}
forecast_growth <- function(train, test) {
  X <- test
  for (v in predictors) {
    f <- as.formula(paste(v, "~ Year + Qrtr"))
    X[[v]] <- predict(lm(f, data = train), newdata = test)
  }
  growth_fit <- lm(PctGrowth ~ Income + Production + Savings + Unemployment,
                   data = train)
  predict(growth_fit, newdata = X)
}

holdout_results <- function(cut_year) {
  tr <- data_all %>% filter(Year < cut_year)
  te <- data_all %>% filter(Year >= cut_year)

  known_fit <- lm(PctGrowth ~ Income + Production + Savings + Unemployment,
                  data = tr)

  tibble(
    holdout         = paste0(cut_year, "-2024"),
    n_quarters      = nrow(te),
    mae_model       = mae(te$PctGrowth, forecast_growth(tr, te)),
    mae_if_X_known  = mae(te$PctGrowth, predict(known_fit, newdata = te)),
    mae_mean_only   = mae(te$PctGrowth, mean(tr$PctGrowth))
  )
}

bind_rows(holdout_results(2024), holdout_results(2020)) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("mae"), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

```{r}
current_model <- lm(PctGrowth ~ Income + Production + Savings + Unemployment,
                    data = data_all)
summary(current_model)
```

```{r}
data_all <- data_all %>%
```

```{r}
lm_income     <- lm(Income ~ Year + Qrtr,       data = data_all)
lm_production <- lm(Production ~ Year + Qrtr,   data = data_all)
lm_savings    <- lm(Savings ~ Year + Qrtr,      data = data_all)
lm_unemp      <- lm(Unemployment ~ Year + Qrtr, data = data_all)

# Predict using future_all (which holds only Q3 and Q4)
data_2025 <- future_all %>%
  mutate(
    Income       = predict(lm_income, newdata = future_all),
    Production   = predict(lm_production, newdata = future_all),
    Savings      = predict(lm_savings, newdata = future_all),
    Unemployment = predict(lm_unemp, newdata = future_all)
  )

predictions_2025 <- predict(current_model, newdata = data_2025,
                            interval = "prediction")

data_2025 <- data_2025 %>%
  mutate(Predicted_PctGrowth = predictions_2025[, "fit"],
         Lower_PI_old = predictions_2025[, "lwr"],
         Upper_PI_old = predictions_2025[, "upr"])

# Simulation interval that includes uncertainty in the forecasted predictors
pred_models <- list(Income = lm_income, Production = lm_production,
                    Savings = lm_savings, Unemployment = lm_unemp)
pred_resids <- sapply(pred_models, residuals)
beta <- coef(current_model)
growth_resids <- residuals(current_model)

set.seed(469)
B <- 5000

# Dynamically map over the remaining future quarters
quarters_to_predict <- as.numeric(as.character(data_2025$Qrtr))

sim_summary <- map_dfr(1:nrow(data_2025), function(i) {
  q_val <- quarters_to_predict[i]
  idx <- sample(nrow(pred_resids), B, replace = TRUE)
  base <- unlist(data_2025[i, predictors])
  
  Xq <- sweep(pred_resids[idx, predictors], 2, base, "+")
  sims <- as.vector(cbind(1, Xq) %*% beta) +
    sample(growth_resids, B, replace = TRUE)
  
  tibble(Qrtr = q_val,
         Lower_PI_sim = quantile(sims, 0.025),
         Upper_PI_sim = quantile(sims, 0.975))
}) %>% mutate(Qrtr = factor(Qrtr, levels = levels(data_all$Qrtr)))

data_2025 <- left_join(data_2025, sim_summary, by = "Qrtr")
print(data_2025 %>%
        select(Year, Qrtr, Predicted_PctGrowth, starts_with("Lower"),
               starts_with("Upper")))
```

```{r}
#sarima

sarima_forecast_X <- function(train, h) {
  X <- sapply(predictors, function(v) {
    as.numeric(forecast(auto.arima(ts_of(train[[v]], train), seasonal = TRUE), h = h)$mean)
  })
  matrix(X, nrow = h, dimnames = list(NULL, predictors))
}

sarima_forecast <- function(train, future) {
  h        <- nrow(future)
  X_future <- sarima_forecast_X(train, h)
  fit <- auto.arima(ts_of(train$PctGrowth, train),
                    xreg = as.matrix(train[, predictors]), seasonal = TRUE)
  fc <- forecast(fit, xreg = X_future, h = h, level = 95)

  list(fit = fit, X_future = X_future,
       out = tibble(Year = future$Year, Qrtr = future$Qrtr, Model = "SARIMA + xreg",
                    Predicted = as.numeric(fc$mean),
                    Lower_95  = as.numeric(fc$lower), Upper_95  = as.numeric(fc$upper)))
}
```

```{r}
fit_prophet <- function(df, regressors = NULL) {
  m <- prophet(weekly.seasonality = FALSE, daily.seasonality = FALSE,
               yearly.seasonality = 2, interval.width = 0.95, fit = FALSE)
  for (r in regressors) m <- add_regressor(m, r)
  suppressMessages(fit.prophet(m, df))
}

prophet_forecast_X <- function(train, future) {
  out <- map(predictors, function(v) {
    m <- fit_prophet(train %>% transmute(ds, y = .data[[v]]))
    predict(m, future %>% select(ds))$yhat
  })
  names(out) <- predictors
  as_tibble(out)
}

prophet_forecast <- function(train, future, seed = 469) {
  set.seed(seed)
  X_future <- prophet_forecast_X(train, future)
  m <- fit_prophet(train %>% select(ds, y, all_of(predictors)), regressors = predictors)
  pred <- predict(m, bind_cols(future %>% select(ds), X_future))

  list(model = m, X_future = X_future,
       out = tibble(Year = future$Year, Qrtr = future$Qrtr, Model = "Prophet + regressors",
                    Predicted = pred$yhat,
                    Lower_95  = pred$yhat_lower, Upper_95  = pred$yhat_upper))
}
```

```{r}
holdout_sarima_prophet <- function(cut_year) {
  tr <- data_all %>% filter(Year <  cut_year)
  te <- data_all %>% filter(Year >= cut_year)

  sar <- sarima_forecast(tr, te)$out$Predicted
  pro <- prophet_forecast(tr, te)$out$Predicted

  tibble(holdout = paste0(cut_year, "-", max(te$Year)),
         n_quarters = nrow(te),
         mae_sarima  = mae(te$PctGrowth, sar),
         mae_prophet = mae(te$PctGrowth, pro))
}

comparison_new <- bind_rows(holdout_sarima_prophet(2024), holdout_sarima_prophet(2020)) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("mae"), ~ round(.x, 3)))
comparison_new
```

```{r}
# Extract the four predictor coefficients and their standard errors
coefficient_table <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    predictor = predictors,
    model = "MLR",
    estimate = as.numeric(coef(current_model)[predictors]),
    se = sqrt(diag(vcov(current_model)))[predictors]
  ),
  tibble(
    predictor = predictors,
    model = "SARIMA",
    estimate = as.numeric(coef(sarima_final$fit)[predictors]),
    se = sqrt(diag(sarima_final$fit$var.coef))[predictors]
  )
)

# Vary each predictor over its observed range
relationship_data <- map_dfr(predictors, function(variable) {

  values <- seq(
    min(data_all[[variable]]),
    max(data_all[[variable]]),
    length.out = 100
  )

  reference <- median(data_all[[variable]])

  crossing(
    coefficient_table |> filter(predictor == variable),
    value = values
  ) |>
    mutate(
      change = estimate * (value - reference),

      # Approximate 95% confidence intervals for the change
      margin = 1.96 * se * abs(value - reference),
      lower = change - margin,
      upper = change + margin
    )
})

# Plot the four relationships for both models
ggplot(
  relationship_data,
  aes(x = value, y = change, color = model, fill = model)
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray60"
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    alpha = 0.15,
    color = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = model)) +
    scale_linewidth_manual(
    values = c("MLR" = 1.5, "SARIMA" = 1),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Predictor Relationships with Company Growth",
    subtitle = "Change relative to each predictor's median",
    x = "Predictor value (original units)",
    y = "Predicted change in PctGrowth",
    color = "Model",
    fill = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
preferred_model <- "MLR"

variable_labels <- c(
  Income = "the disposable-income growth indicator",
  Production = "the US production growth indicator",
  Savings = "the personal savings change indicator",
  Unemployment = "the unemployment-rate change indicator"
)

board_results <- coefficient_table |>
  filter(model == preferred_model) |>
  mutate(
    lower = estimate - 1.96 * se,
    upper = estimate + 1.96 * se,

    statement = if_else(
      lower <= 0 & upper >= 0,
      
      # What prints if the interval crosses zero (not significant)
      paste0(
        "Changes in ", 
        variable_labels[predictor], 
        " do not have a statistically significant relationship with quarterly company growth in this model, as the confidence interval includes zero."
      ),
      
      # What prints if the interval does NOT cross zero (significant)
      paste0(
        "A one-unit increase in ",
        variable_labels[predictor],
        " is associated with ",
        sprintf("%.3f", abs(estimate)),
        " percentage points ",
        if_else(estimate >= 0, "higher", "lower"),
        " predicted quarterly company growth, ",
        "holding the other predictors fixed."
      )
    )
  )

# Coefficients and approximate 95% confidence intervals
board_results |>
  select(predictor, estimate, lower, upper)

cat(paste(board_results$statement, collapse = "\n\n"))
```
```{r}
#| cache: true

# Keep observations in chronological order
evaluation_data <- data_all |> arrange(ds)

# Start after 40 quarters of training data.
# Stop where two future observations are still available.
cutoffs <- seq(40, nrow(evaluation_data) - 2)

forecast_errors <- map_dfr(cutoffs, function(i) {
  
  # Only observations available at this historical cutoff
  train <- evaluation_data[1:i, ]
  
  # The next two quarters
  test <- evaluation_data[(i + 1):(i + 2), ]
  
  # Forecast using all three methods
  mlr_predictions <- forecast_growth(train, test)
  sarima_predictions <- sarima_forecast(train, test)$out$Predicted
  prophet_predictions <- prophet_forecast(train, test)$out$Predicted
  
  tibble(
    cutoff = evaluation_data$ds[i],
    horizon = 1:2,
    actual = test$PctGrowth,
    mlr_error = actual - as.numeric(mlr_predictions),
    sarima_error = actual - as.numeric(sarima_predictions),
    prophet_error = actual - as.numeric(prophet_predictions)
  )
})
```

```{r}
# Compare average absolute errors for all three models
forecast_errors |>
  group_by(horizon) |>
  summarise(
    MLR_MAE = mean(abs(mlr_error)),
    SARIMA_MAE = mean(abs(sarima_error)),
    PROPHET_MAE = mean(abs(prophet_error)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# One-quarter-ahead comparisons
errors_h1 <- forecast_errors |> filter(horizon == 1)

# MLR vs SARIMA (h=1)
dm.test(
  errors_h1$mlr_error,
  errors_h1$sarima_error,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  h = 1,
  power = 1,
  varestimator = "bartlett"
)

# MLR vs Prophet (h=1)
dm.test(
  errors_h1$mlr_error,
  errors_h1$prophet_error,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  h = 1,
  power = 1,
  varestimator = "bartlett"
)

# Two-quarter-ahead comparisons
errors_h2 <- forecast_errors |> filter(horizon == 2)

# MLR vs SARIMA (h=2)
dm.test(
  errors_h2$mlr_error,
  errors_h2$sarima_error,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  h = 2,
  power = 1,
  varestimator = "bartlett"
)

# MLR vs Prophet (h=2)
dm.test(
  errors_h2$mlr_error,
  errors_h2$prophet_error,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  h = 2,
  power = 1,
  varestimator = "bartlett"
)
```

# PRESENTATION NOTES FOR MATTHEW

## Slide 1: Current Forecasting Strategy & 2025 Outlook
**The Current Method:** 
Our team currently relies on a Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) model to project VistaLux’s quarterly growth. This model operates by taking a "snapshot" of four major macroeconomic indicators—consumer disposable income, US production, personal savings, and unemployment—to estimate our company's growth in that exact same quarter. 

**2025 Forecasting Strategy:**
Because 2025 hasn't happened yet, we do not have the actual economic indicator data needed to plug into the MLR model. To solve this, we used a two-stage forecasting method:
1. First, we independently forecasted the four macroeconomic indicators for Q3 and Q4 of 2025. 
2. Next, we fed those forecasted economic estimates into our MLR model to generate our final company growth projections.

**2025 Projections:**
Using this method, our projected company growth is **0.768%** for Q3 2025 and **0.657%** for Q4 2025. 

## Slide 2: Exploring Alternative Models
To ensure we are using the most accurate forecasting methods, the data team explored two advanced alternatives to our current MLR model:
1. **SARIMA (Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average):** Unlike MLR, which only looks at a single quarter in isolation, SARIMA looks at the company's past growth momentum. It accounts for historical trends and repeating seasonal cycles (e.g., Q4 holiday spikes) while still factoring in the economic indicators.
2. **Prophet:** Developed by Meta, this is a highly flexible additive model. It excels at adapting to shifting trendlines over time and handles missing data or outliers more smoothly than strict linear models, while still allowing us to add the four economic indicators as custom regressors.

## Slide 3: Model Performance & Recommendation
**The Testing Method:**
To determine which model performs best, we ran a "rolling origin" simulation. We stepped back through the company's history, hiding future data, and asked each model to predict the next one and two quarters. We then calculated the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for all three models. 

**The Verdict:**
The current MLR model consistently produced the lowest average forecast error (0.439 at a 1-quarter horizon and 0.438 at a 2-quarter horizon). While SARIMA and Prophet are highly sophisticated, statistical tests (Diebold-Mariano) confirmed they did not provide a statistically significant improvement in forecasting accuracy over our current method. 

**Recommendation:** 
Because the advanced models failed to demonstrate a clear predictive advantage, we recommend continuing with the MLR model. Its straightforward structure makes it much easier to explain exactly how the broader economy is impacting VistaLux's bottom line.

## Slide 4: Economic Relationships & Limitations
Holding all other variables constant, our MLR model estimates the following relationships:
* A one-unit increase in the disposable-income indicator is associated with a **0.741 percentage point increase** in quarterly growth.
* A one-unit increase in the US production indicator is associated with a **0.047 percentage point increase** in quarterly growth.
* A one-unit increase in the personal savings indicator is associated with a **0.053 percentage point decrease** in quarterly growth.
* Changes in unemployment do not have a statistically significant relationship with our growth.

**Statistical Limitations:**
While these estimates provide a strong baseline, the board should view the exact confidence intervals with slight caution. Our residual diagnostic tests indicate that the MLR model errors are somewhat correlated over time and exhibit uneven variance, meaning the model's exact precision bounds may be overly optimistic.
